theme: The Triumphal Entry; Temple cleansing; the wicked tenants
readingInstruction: Read Matthew 21:1-22:14. Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey, cleanses the temple, curses a fig tree, is challenged on his authority, and tells three parables of judgment. Read the entry in light of Zechariah 9:9, which you memorized last unit.
settingTheScene: This is the beginning of the final week of Jesus’ earthly life. He enters Jerusalem to the shouts of the crowds, and what follows is a series of confrontations in and around the temple. The religious leaders, who see him as a threat, try to trap him. Jesus responds with parables that expose their rejection of God’s messengers and of his Son.
observation: “Behold, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey” (21:5).
“Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” (21:9).
“My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you make it a den of robbers” (21:13).
“By what authority are you doing these things?” (21:23).
“But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves, This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance” (21:38).
“The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (21:42).
“Therefore I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits” (21:43).
“For many are called, but few are chosen” (22:14).
interpretation:
Jesus plans his entry. He sends for a donkey and a colt, and Matthew says this fulfilled the prophecy of Zechariah 9:9, the verse you memorized at the end of Unit 14. The king comes humble and on a donkey. The crowds spread cloaks and branches, and shout “Hosanna,” which means “save us,” quoting Psalm 118. They see him as the Son of David.

He goes straight to the temple and drives out the merchants. The temple was meant to be a house of prayer for all nations, and it had become a marketplace. He heals the blind and lame there, and the children shout his praise, while the leaders are indignant.

The cursed fig tree is a parable in action. It had leaves, which promised fruit, but no fruit. It pictures a religion with outward show and no reality. The leaders then challenge his authority, and he answers with a question about John’s baptism that they cannot answer without exposing themselves.

The parable of the two sons shows that tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the kingdom ahead of the religious leaders, because they repented. The parable of the wicked tenants is the clearest. The landowner sends servants, who are beaten and killed, and finally he sends his son. The tenants kill him to seize the inheritance. Jesus quotes Psalm 118: the stone the builders rejected becomes the cornerstone. The leaders perceive that he is speaking about them.

The wedding feast is the last parable. Those invited refuse, and the invitation goes out to everyone. But one man arrives without a wedding garment, and he is cast out. The garment pictures what God provides for entry. “Many are called, but few are chosen.”
connection: Zechariah 9:9 and Psalm 118:25-26 stand behind the entry. Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11 are quoted at the temple cleansing. Isaiah 5:1-7 is the background to the vineyard parable. Psalm 118:22-23 is the cornerstone passage, also cited in Acts 4:11 and 1 Peter 2:4-8. Isaiah 61:10 speaks of being clothed with garments of salvation. Revelation 19:7-9 describes the marriage supper of the Lamb. Galatians 3:27: as many as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.
application:
Welcome Jesus as the king who comes humbly. Is there an area where you want a more impressive king?

Ask whether your life has leaves without fruit. What is one practical step toward real fruit?

Think about the wedding garment: are you trusting in your own righteousness or in the clothing Christ provides?
prayerPrompts: Say “Hosanna” to the Son of David, and tell him why.
Thank him for coming humbly to Jerusalem.
Ask him to cleanse the temple of your own heart.
